trova: This book rests on a particular order of priorities, and the patient comes first. The night covering provider and the rapid response team would have read Nadia's 19:25 entry long before any attorney saw it. It would have told them how Mr. Jensen looked earlier in the evening, what had already been tried and what limits had been set. A note written for the next clinician serves the patient best. It is usually also the note that holds up best with every other reader.

trova: Only after that does the note serve your license and your career, and it does so in one way: by making your reasoning visible. It cannot make a wrong decision right. It cannot stop a family from filing a claim, or anyone from filing a complaint. A note written mainly to protect its author tends to read that way, crowded with boilerplate and self-justification, and the readers in this chapter spot it quickly. What a careful note offers is narrower, and more reliable. It lets people who arrive already knowing the ending see the moment you were in: what you knew, what you did not know yet, and why you chose what you chose.

trova: Every scenario chapter follows the same order. It opens with a constructed scenario: a named clinician, a setting, a patient and the clock. Next comes what the record will be asked: the short set of questions that a claim, a complaint or a review would bring to that kind of encounter. Then comes the weak note, written the way a competent, busy NP might write it: accurate as far as it goes, but thin.

trova: Beside it is the defensible rewrite of the same encounter. Nothing is added that the clinician did not do, so the difference lies in the writing and not in the care. When a patient is walking out or a page is waiting, the list is the part to reach for.

trova: Patients have a legal right to their records, and under the federal information-blocking rules in force since 2021, most US providers may not withhold signed notes without a recognized exception, so many notes reach the patient portal as soon as they are signed. As the chapter on where claims begin noted, a complaint needs no injury behind it.

trova: Mr. Eckert takes sertraline for depression and sleeps with CPAP for obstructive sleep apnea. He drinks two or three beers on weekend evenings and lives with his wife, who drove him in, and their sixteen-year-old son. Ibuprofen at 16:30 brings his pain from 8 out of 10 to 6, and at 17:00 he asks: "Ibuprofen won't get me through the night. Can I get a Percocet?" At 17:05 Audrey searches the **prescription drug monitoring program**, or PDMP, the state's database of dispensed prescriptions for controlled drugs such as oxycodone. Then she prescribes ten tablets of oxycodone 5 mg beside scheduled ibuprofen and acetaminophen, not the Percocet he named.

trova: Ask the attorney, first, whom they represent: you, your employer or both. If those interests could diverge, ask whether you need counsel of your own. Then ask about deadlines, what happens next and your part in it, whom you may talk to about the event, and whether and how to write down what you remember.
